# Extraction notes (working ledger, written while reading originals)
Text extraction: pdftotext -layout (PDF), textutil (DOCX), copy (MD). Page = PDF page per form-feed.

## S05 Packaging (Thumbnail_Title) - SOP(1).pdf — 1 page, 340 words, no author/date
- Viewer looks at thumbnail first, then title; decision "in less than a second, milliseconds".
- "Goal: The goal is to get a click (10%+ CTR)". Prescribed, untested target.
- Steps: 1 know audience (who, what looking for); 2 research: screenshots/notes of similar-niche packaging; 3 genuine, no fake attention; "Realistic & Genuine packaging = more clicks"; autoplay => "first 10 seconds of your video heavily impacts your CTR (video's first 10 secs is the new packaging)".
- Thumbnail: bright & natural colors; bold big fonts, less text; sell 1 BIG idea; look realistic/believable.
- Title: fewer characters (1 sentence); broad topic => shorter title; narrow => longer/specific.
- Improve: never perfect; get feedback on every video's packaging before final; "Hitting Audience Desire > Design".
- Duration must match packaging (10-min video should not look like documentary). Viewer should recognise type/length from packaging.
- "How was your last video? Did the viewer enjoy your last video? It impacts the click."
- Note: the "first 10 seconds affects CTR" claim: Home autoplay (inline playback) exists; official CTR definition counts impressions on thumbnails; claim UNVERIFIED as stated.

## S11 Viral Checklist.pdf — 2 pages, attributed to Codie Sanchez
- Framing: "not about checking every box — but the more you hit, the higher your odds". Prescribed, no data.
- 11 items with examples: 1 Audience pain point; 2 Promise of transformation; 3 Evoke emotion; 4 Contrarian thinking ("College is a scam"); 5 Specificity & numbers ("$18,472.12 in one week"); 6 Urgency/timeliness ("won't exist in 2026"); 7 Experience & familiarity (personal story); 8 Motivate; 9 Concise; 10 Enhancer words (secret, money, mistake); 11 Credibility hack (famous names: Elon Musk, Taylor Swift, Apple).
- Items 5, 6, 10 testable against YIOS title features (money amount H01, urgency, threat words).

## S08 The Magic of 'BUT' and 'THEREFORE' in Storytelling.docx (1).pdf — 3 pages
- Is an LLM chat response ("Got it — I've successfully absorbed...") summarising a mind map; AI_INTERPRETATION container around a known craft principle.
- p1: Trey Parker & Matt Stone (South Park) rule: replace "AND THEN" with "BUT" (conflict/complication) or "THEREFORE" (consequence/resolution). Example "Fridge broke down (BUT) had to buy new one (THEREFORE)". Tips: avoid "and then"; find conflict points; follow with logical consequences. Benefits: momentum, engagement, curiosity.
- p1 table row 7: alternate BUT → THEREFORE "every 8–12 seconds" (LLM's own application, not from Parker/Stone).
- p2: example medical: "(0:00) Patient collapses during routine walk — BUT doctors intervene with emergency angioplasty — THEREFORE ..."; VEO mapping: BUT = camera shift/sudden cut/tonal contrast; THEREFORE = smooth dolly, warm light, resolution music.
- p2–3 "Fusion Framework v2.0 — The Science of Storytelling for YouTube (CTR, AVD, Retention)": CTR engineering = title/thumbnail as compressed micro-story (conflict + curiosity gap (Loewenstein) + emotion); AVD engineering = tension–release micro-arcs "every 2–3 minutes"; Retention engineering = payoff + tease next loop at end; "Emotion > Information"; "Curiosity, dopamine, and suspense science control retention"; attention dips "≈ every 2.5–3 min"; peak–end effect; "Mirror Neurons"; "YouTube's recommendation system = behavioral psychology engine".
- p3 example Niagara Falls through a straw: 0:00–0:30 cold open (BUT) / 1:30 micro-arc (THEREFORE) / 3:30 escalation (BUT) / 8:00 payoff (THEREFORE). "Installed 2025-10-20" (dated LLM claim).
- Contradiction inside one file: BUT/THEREFORE every 8–12 s vs micro-arcs every 2–3 min (different granularity; neither tested).

B angle lenses (15): revelation, hidden danger, identity, mistake, contradiction, prediction, consequence, comeback, transformation, social comparison, warning signal, myth vs reality, investigation, experience/POV, completeness; per angle: core event, emotional trigger, viewer question, promised payoff, visual proof opportunity, factual risk. C packaging before production (title & thumbnail one system; title responsibilities; thumbnail: one dominant idea at mobile size, one subject/conflict/focal action, complement not repeat title; composition: rule of thirds, centered symmetry, leading lines, triangular, S-curve, golden ratio; "three meaningfully different packaging hypotheses"). D hooks: 12 families (contrarian, curiosity, action, novel-insight, live demonstration, skill showcase, challenge, amazement, shock (responsibly), pain-to-transformation, identity, prediction); three-beat engine Context Lean → Scroll-Stop Interjection → Contrarian Snapback; enhancers (proof early, short sentences, visual+spoken+on-screen, early value sample, promise present, one primary loop + at most one secondary); never begin with greeting/biography/long disclaimer. E spine SETUP → BUT → THEREFORE → BUT → THEREFORE → ESCALATION → PAYOFF → ECHO/NEXT STEP; five per-section questions. F retention: "Do not insert random pattern breaks on a timer" (contradicts S17 #6 20–30 s, S06); reset types (12); retention map (promise confirmation, first proof, first escalation, midpoint re-hook, strongest evidence, payoff, summary, next-video bridge); protect against repetition, premature answer, excessive withholding, etc. G human connection (Casey-style; physical props; useful imperfection; "So what?"; constraints). H production blueprint list (beat sheet, storyboard, A/B-roll, proof list, on-screen text, medical graphics, sound arc, thumbnail capture list, fact-check, disclosure checklist); every visual must clarify/prove/escalate/emotionally translate/reset. I SEO by traffic source (search-led vs browse/suggested-led) + publishing checklist (first two description lines, captions, chapters, audience/language/disclosure settings, end screen tied to next question, pinned comment, playlists, no misleading tags). J analytics + 6-step diagnosis ladder (low impressions → topic/audience; impressions low clicks → packaging; clicks early drop → promise/intro; middle decline → escalation; good retention weak loyalty → personality; high views low satisfaction → overpromise); "Change one major variable at a time".

- §7 Deep research protocol; §8 input contract; §9 14-part output contract; §10 15-dimension 1–10 scoring "Do not average blindly"; failure in truthfulness/safety/promise/visual clarity disqualifies.
- §11 Anti-patterns incl. "Force every title under an arbitrary character count" (vs S12 55-char), "Stretch videos to eight minutes", "Use cards or resets at fixed timestamps", "Claim AI disclosure reduces reach".

## S16 🎯 YouTube Video SEO – COMPLETE CHECKLIST DOCUMENT (1).pdf — 13 pages
- p1 purpose: ranking, discoverability, impressions, clicks, views. One-line "This video helps ___ audience to ___."
- p2 main keyword via YouTube autosuggest, VidIQ, TubeBuddy, Google Trends; 1 primary + 3–5 secondary; volume, medium/low competition, clear intent. Example "how to lose belly fat at home".
- p2–3 analyze top 5 ranking videos (titles, thumbnails, descriptions, views, upload date); "Can I make something better?" else change keyword.
- p3–4 script: keyword naturally in first 30 s; "Repeat keyword 2–3 times in video"; related terms.
- p4 quality: clear audio, lighting, "HD quality (1080p minimum)", no silent gaps, engaging intro; "YouTube ranks good content higher". Retention: first 10 s hook, no long intro, fast pacing, chapters, B-roll, subtitles; "High retention = better ranking".
- p4–5 Title "MOST IMPORTANT SEO element": keyword at beginning; "Under 60 characters"; emotional; clear benefit; formula Primary Keyword + Benefit + Curiosity; avoid ALL CAPS, clickbait, vague, stuffing.
- p6 description: keyword in first 25 words; first 2 lines most important; 200–300+ words; keyword 2–3 times; timestamps, links.
- p7 tags: main keyword first; 10–20 tags; channel name tag; no competitor names. (Official: tags minor; misspellings.)
- p8 "CTR = HUGE ranking factor"; thumbnail: custom, high contrast, big bold text, "3–5 words only", emotional expression, matches title; mistakes: "No face", boring colors.
- p9 settings: category, language, subtitles, end screens, cards, chapters, pinned comment, hashtags, location.
- p9–10 ask to like/comment/subscribe; reply/pin/heart; "Engage in first 24 hours".
- p10–11 share to Facebook/Instagram/WhatsApp/Twitter/LinkedIn, embed in blog, communities; playlists.
- p11 "After 48 hours check: CTR (aim 6–12%), Retention (40%+), AVD, traffic sources"; if low change title/thumbnail/description/"Add better tags".
- p12–13 golden rules: never fake tags, misleading titles, buy views, stuffing; humans first SEO second; "SEO helps you get impressions. But CONTENT QUALITY makes you win."
- Contradictions: S05 CTR 10%+ vs S16 6–12% vs YouTube Help "half of all channels ... 2%–10%"; S12 55 chars vs S16 60 chars vs S14 "arbitrary character count" anti-pattern; S16 "No face" a mistake vs S14 "facial expression only when emotionally truthful".

## S09 The Ultimate Nano-Banana Prompt Guide.docx — not paginated (DOCX), 754 words; LLM-authored ("Absolutely! ✅")
- Image-generation prompt structure (8 mandatory slots): Subject, Action/Pose, Environment, Lighting & Mood, Camera & Composition, Style, Details, Output format & intent. Example: young doctor outside hospital, 85 mm, 4:5.
- Best practices: hyper-specific, visual intent first, control camera, preserve physics (matching shadows), identity consistency ("Same subject as previous image"), conversational refinement.
- Editing verbs (one per instruction): replace background, remove/add object, change outfit, adjust lighting, enhance details, maintain identity, resize/recompose, apply style, composite.
- "Semantic negative prompts": describe the opposite desired scene rather than "No cars".
- Camera glossary (shot type, angle, lens, focus, composition); lighting glossary; style system ("Pick 1"); output config (aspect ratio, resolution, "Use SynthID watermark allowed").
- Relevance: thumbnail/visual production tooling. Not YouTube performance evidence. Synthetic realistic imagery triggers YouTube altered/synthetic disclosure duty when realistic (check per use).

## S10 Ultimate Google VEO 3 Prompt Guide for VIRAL Videos.docx — 3,747 words; an LLM summary of a separate PDF (the PDF itself is NOT in the repo: EXTERNAL_ONLY/NOT_FOUND)
- Capabilities as stated (vendor facts, dated mid-2025, not re-verified): 720p native → 1080p upscale; 8 s max per clip; native dialogue/ambient audio (text-to-video only); ~100 credits per HQ clip; SynthID watermark; access via Gemini or Flow.
- Prompt formula: [CHARACTER]+[ACTION]+[CAMERA ANGLE]+[LIGHTING]+[GENRE/STYLE]+[MOTION]+[ENVIRONMENT]+[COLOR PALETTE] (+ dialogue, tone, ambient). Dialogue: no quote marks (can trigger subtitles); 1–2 background sounds max.
- Character consistency: repeat base description verbatim; reference images / Frames-to-Video.
- Camera grammar: eye-level neutral; low angle = power; high angle = vulnerable; OTS = intimacy; POV/selfie = immersion; pan/tilt/dolly/zoom/tracking/crane/handheld. Write motion with durations ("dolly in slowly (1.2s)").
- "Viral templates" for "high-CTR short-form videos": Bigfoot vlogs, ASMR slicing, Stormtrooper vlogs, animal olympics, street interviews, cinematic animal shorts (no evidence for "high-CTR").
- JSON prompting for repeatability; workflow: scene table → style sheet → prompts → cheap drafts → HQ render → stitch in CapCut.
- Doctor example in Urdu about semaglutide/NAION ("NAION is very rare") — applied medical use case; production of a realistic synthetic doctor requires YouTube altered/synthetic content disclosure and medical accuracy review.
- Colour/emotion: warm golden = nostalgic/hopeful; cold blue = isolation/tension; neon = futuristic.

## S02 Hook (1).pdf ≡ S03 Hook guide.pdf — 58 pages each; extracted text byte-identical (pdftotext output cmp equal); PDF SHA-256 differ (4129b2… vs 4bbe6c…, 682,676 vs 682,682 bytes). ONE source, two containers. Content = sequence of LLM chat responses ("Excellent — this is a goldmine", "Locked. I've folded...") summarising ~9 unnamed creator videos + comment threads + an embedded third-party "Viral Hook Vault™" (Respected Creator community; sales CTA p27). Mostly short-form (IG Reels/TikTok) and Meta ads, not YouTube long-form.
- p1–3 "3-Step Hook Formula (Mega Tip)": 1 Context Lean (topic clarity + common ground/benefit/pain/metaphor/mind-blowing; "Oh, this is about me"); 2 Scroll Stop Interjection (contrastive word but/however/yet; "prediction error system — curiosity spikes"); 3 Contrarian Snapback (twist reversing assumption, on-topic; "Surprise + uncertainty create dopamine-driven curiosity"). Example Vegas Sphere: "biggest screen ... 20x larger than an IMAX" → "but ... the screen is actually the least impressive part" → "the most impressive part is the audio".
- p3–5 five enhancers: 4 visual hooks (3–5 bold words on screen, just-enough motion; visuals+text+voice "= highest retention"; "Humans process visuals faster than audio"); 5 "People like hearing this" benefit-first (magnesium → better sleep); 6 Cult hopping (familiar brands/celebrities; Taylor Swift); 7 Compress speed to value ("within 4 seconds (short form) or 1–2 minutes (long form)"); 8 Staccato sentences then lengthen.
- p5 psychological drivers table: curiosity, pattern interruption, relevance, familiarity, instant value, brevity, visual stimulation.
- p6–7 from comments: anecdote "300k IG views in 3 days"; hook definition "A sentence that creates one or more questions the viewer cannot answer"; audio hooks (whoosh at snapback); re-hook cadence; "Make the gap, then fill the gap"; trust/"reciprocity debt" as meta-hook; over-gesturing fatigue; snapback that teases a different topic → viewers bail; keep value high around CTAs.
- p7–9 QA: hook window "0–4s short / 0–30s long"; "Micro re-hooks every 15–30s"; sensory schedule 0:00–0:03 title + snapback word; 0:04–0:08 first value hit; integrity: "Pay off the exact curiosity you created", CTA on value. 12-item 1–5 rubric "(≥ 45 total generally predicts strong hold)" — unsupported threshold.
- p9–14 second video: curiosity gap, pattern interrupt, stakes, specificity, authority transfer, time constraint; "3 hooks per video (split-test)" posting to sub-accounts, read in 24–72 h; 5 formulas: Mistake Reveal, Counterintuitive Truth, Transformation Tease, Urgent Warning ("per new policy/algorithm change"), Secret Reveal; visual hook stack; split-test SOP measuring hold @3s/5s/8s, AVD, saves/shares; 10 niche examples (e.g. finance "The tax mistake consultants make every April that costs $18,400" — illustrative, invented numbers).

### T39 "YouTube Algorithm 2026 — What Creators Need to Know" (Creator Insider; Todd Beaupré, YouTube senior director of growth & discovery; Rene Ritchie, creator liaison) — FIRST-PARTY SPOKEN (YouTube employees, official Creator Insider channel), video rHLjxrbXmmY. Key points (transcript wording):
- Ch2: "most of the recommendations are more pulled for each viewer"; activated "when a viewer opens their app or turns on their TV"; considers what they've watched, "what time of day ... which device"; "brings in candidate videos ... and then ranks them for that viewer. And so each viewer gets a different ranking".
- Ch3: majority of audience can be non-subscribers "even in the first hour"; "It's learning for different audiences. So, it can learn that for subscribers, this video is not ... performing well and for people who haven't watched the channel, it is."
- Ch4: "we're not basing decisions just on those initial moments"; "a lot of videos also get the majority of their views ... a month or ... later. If it's evergreen content, we're not going to stop"; experiments capping repeat recommendation ("not ... more than eight times"); context (TV evening for hour-long videos).
- Ch5: "our north star is ... long-term user value"; "no metric on its own is a good indicator of value"; "for a viral video, like clickthrough rate and average view duration will go down as the views go up" (broader audience lowers aggregates); "it's not always that the time you spent is valued which is why we also bring in the surveys"; absolute AND relative watch time; likes, dislikes, comments — none sufficient alone; "there isn't a ... weighting for each of these that is the same for everyone ... not ... the same for you at all times"; TV vs mobile factor differences; advice: compare videos relative to similar-length videos, retention graphs, like rates, "listen to your audiences".
- Ch5: comments off / ads off are not penalised ("we didn't penalize people that ... choose not to have comments on").
- Ch6: "the system isn't trying to find a single category for your content ... we are very video centric"; "puddles don't cause rain" — YouTube isn't pushing longer videos; TV viewers want them and the system follows.
- Ch7: larger desktop homepage thumbnails "drove more attention and engagement around long form"; "hundreds of experiments ... running at any given time".
- Ch8: topic switches have different audiences/view potentials; patience in new areas.
- Ch9: "align channels with audiences"; cross-channel recommendation exists; within-channel the system distinguishes format/length/topic per viewer; Shorts/long/podcasts/live can coexist — matched to viewer interest.
- Ch10: suggested traffic is personalized, not only "related"; "the number one place that people are watching videos from channels they're subscribed to is actually on the watch page in that suggested list".
- Ch11: new channels: "parts of the system that don't depend on ... history with that channel ... user's topical preferences and what we understand about what this video is about"; "if we don't, then maybe that video just won't get more impressions"; YouTube tracks how many videos get a chance and creator sustainability.
- Ch11–12: homepage ranking weights homepage-context behaviour; embed/ad/link traffic down-weighted if not predictive; "I wouldn't advise people to turn off ... notifying subscribers"; "not going to decide just based on the first hour or first 10,000 people".
- Ch12–13: Subscriptions-feed traffic source = "a clean way to isolate the content from the algorithm"; "probably all your videos have about maybe a 10% or less click-through rate" in the subs feed → "90% of the time, your subscribed audience isn't deciding to watch" → normal; "the portion of their audience that watches every video is so tiny".
